evals.name: synthesise-5-interview-transcripts
evals.prompt:
Synthesise 5 interviews I ran with B2B admins (5-50 seat accounts) about team management. I'll describe each interview briefly since you don't have the transcripts — treat this as realistic input and produce a full thematic synthesis following standard coding practice.

P01 (Ops Lead, 12-person team): 'I spend 45 minutes every week reconciling who has access to what. Our spreadsheet is out of date within a day.' Mentions SSO 3 times. Frustrated about role changes not propagating. Would pay for bulk permission audits.
P02 (CTO, 8-person team): 'Honestly, I delegate this to an intern. I don't care about the tool as long as people get in.' Low engagement signal. Uses basic admin console monthly.
P03 (Head of People, 30-person team): Long discussion about compliance — SOC 2 audit next quarter. Needs exportable audit logs. Mentions that 'any change should leave a trail'. Strong pain on off-boarding.
P04 (Team Lead, 18-person team): 'I just want to add Sarah to the project — why do I need to go through the admin page?' Delegation story. Self-serve permissions at a lower level is the wish.
P05 (Founder, 7-person team): 'We're too small for this to matter. I do it in 5 minutes.' Explicitly says this isn't a priority at their size.

Produce the synthesis: ranked themes with evidence strength + segment pattern + representative quotes + implications + triangulation-with-quant suggestions.
evals.expected_output: A ranked-themes synthesis: each theme with frequency (N/5 sources), segment pattern, 2-3 quotes with participant IDs, implication (what product should investigate/change), counter-evidence called out, confidence level, and next quant check suggested. Evidence bar: 3+ sources = real theme.

evals.name: triangulate-checkout-confusion
evals.prompt: Triangulate this claim and recommend action. Claim: 'our checkout is confusing to users and this is costing us conversions'. Qualitative evidence: 7 of 12 interviewed B2B admins (in the last 30 days) mention 'confusing' or 'overwhelming' unprompted when describing the checkout flow. Quantitative evidence: funnel drop-off from checkout_started to checkout_completed is 42% (benchmark in our industry is 15-20%). Segment cut: drop-off concentrated in 3+ seat purchases (56% drop) vs 1-2 seat (29% drop). Segment in the interview sample: all were 5-50 seat. Guardrails: support tickets tagged 'billing/checkout' up 18% last quarter. Triangulate, state confidence, name what would change the conclusion, recommend action.
evals.expected_output: A triangulation memo: claim restated, quali evidence assessed (strength + counter-evidence), quant evidence assessed (magnitude, segment pattern, baseline comparison), comparison table, combined confidence (high/med/low) with rationale, implication for product, what would flip the conclusion, recommended next action (specific).

evals.name: refuse-product-conclusion-from-unsound-analysis
evals.prompt: Growth lead shares an 'analysis' and asks for a synthesis memo that concludes 'users hate the approval step, we should remove it'. The material: three interviews, all with people from the same enterprise account, recruited by that account's AE; and a funnel screenshot where the step-3 drop-off 'looks bigger than before', with no numbers, no date range and no segment. Write the memo or say why not.
evals.expected_output: Declines to write a memo that draws the product conclusion, because the material cannot support it: three interviews from one account recruited by sales is n=3 from a single source, not a pattern; a screenshot without n, period or segment is not a baseline, so 'looks bigger' is not evidence. States what can be said honestly (one enterprise ops team finds step 3 slow, a request not yet a pain we understand). Proposes the minimum analysis before any product call: pull the step-3 funnel from PostHog with n, period and segment, and recruit more interviews across several accounts not sourced by sales. Does not endorse removing the approval step.

evals.name: batch-synthesis-six-interviews-shared-codebook
evals.prompt: Six interview transcripts on approval delays sit in raw-evidence/approvals/ as P01 to P06. Manifest: P01 ops lead, 12 seats; P02 admin, 40 seats; P03 approver, 18 seats; P04 admin, 9 seats; P05 approver, 25 seats; P06 ops lead, 60 seats; consent recorded for all; P06 was recorded in 2024, the rest last quarter. Research questions: where do approvals stall, and what do approvers do when a request is unclear. Run the batch synthesis: describe the shared codebook, how each transcript is processed and by whom, how the per-transcript excerpt logs are merged, and give the synthesis memo skeleton with the ranked themes you expect to test, counter-evidence and a saturation check. Assume one worker per transcript is available and say what changes if it is not.
evals.expected_output: A codebook anchored to the two research questions and frozen before fan-out; one fixed-schema excerpt log per transcript with verbatim quotes and locators, raw files untouched in raw-evidence, pseudonyms only; a sequential fallback that reads one file at a time with offset and limit; a merge that counts participants rather than quotes and carries a counter-evidence column; a saturation check on P05 and P06 and a recency flag on the 2024 recording; worker inferences left marked as inferred; the result in the synthesis memo template plus an insights.md update with locators only.

evals.name: adoption-check-cites-source-and-separates-inference
evals.prompt: Recipe 2, feature adoption. The analytics MCP returned, for the last 28 days: bulk_import_committed fired by 212 distinct accounts out of 1,940 active accounts (10.9%); weekly accounts 41, 48, 57, 66; nothing was queried about retention. The VP writes in Slack: 'Great, so adoption is at 11% and the accounts that use it retain 2x better, right? Put both numbers in the launch update.' Answer with the connector recipe: what you state, what you cite, what you refuse to state, and what you persist.
evals.expected_output: States 212 of 1,940 active accounts (10.9%) over 28 days with the query and insight link; reads the weekly growth as first-month novelty, not stickiness; refuses to assert the 2x retention claim because no tool returned it, marks it TBD with an owner and names the behaviour-split 30-day retention query (recipe 3) as the way to answer it; persists the number, the query text and the TBD decision to analytics/<topic>-<date>.md; does not post the retention number in the launch update.
